paragraphs: This paper studies the large-matrix behavior of features produced by a neural network with one hidden layer. Its mathematical setup uses random input and weight matrices with independent, identically distributed, centered entries, followed by a smooth nonlinear activation. The object of interest is the spectrum of the resulting feature matrix product: how its eigenvalues are distributed as the matrices grow.

The authors use the resolvent method from random matrix theory, together with a cumulant expansion. They establish an approximate fourth-degree equation for a transform describing the limiting spectrum, recovering an equation previously obtained through moment calculations. They also extend the analysis to an independent, rank-one Gaussian additive bias.

That extension changes an important conclusion. Within the studied bias model, no activation can preserve the singular-value distribution from layer to layer, whereas a simple integral condition suffices without bias. The authors describe their method as less combinatorial and more robust, and suggest it may extend to models where moment-based calculations become intractable.
neurips-2021-analysis-of-one-hidden-laye.tldr: A random-matrix analysis shows how additive bias prevents spectral preservation in the studied single-hidden-layer network model.

paragraphs: Contrastive learning trains a representation by distinguishing similar pairs of examples from dissimilar pairs. Success at this training task does not necessarily mean the representation captures everything useful for later predictions. This paper investigates shortcuts in which the model suppresses important predictive features while still satisfying its contrastive objective.

The authors find that the difficulty of the pair-discrimination task influences which features survive. Making pairs harder can improve the representation of some features, but this improvement can come at the expense of features that were already represented well. The finding makes pair difficulty a tradeoff rather than a straightforward route to richer representations.

To address this behavior, the paper introduces implicit feature modification, or IFM. It alters positive and negative samples to steer the model toward retaining a broader variety of predictive information. Experiments on vision and medical imaging tasks show reduced feature suppression and improved downstream performance. These results support IFM as a way to counter the observed shortcut behavior, without establishing that contrastive learning becomes free of shortcuts in every setting.
neurips-2021-can-contrastive-learning-av.tldr: Implicit feature modification reduces observed contrastive-learning shortcuts by encouraging models to retain more predictive features.

paragraphs: This paper investigates representations for unsupervised segmentation of three-dimensional biomedical images stored as voxel grids. Its central idea is that relationships among smaller image volumes contain an implicit hierarchy. Capturing those relationships can make a representation better suited to segmentation than treating the subvolumes without that structure.

The proposed model is a three-dimensional variational autoencoder whose latent space is hyperbolic. This geometry is used explicitly to represent hierarchical relationships. A new gyroplane convolutional layer maps information from that embedding space back into three-dimensional images, connecting the hierarchical representation to the model's reconstruction task.

The architecture is paired with an additional self-supervised objective beyond the standard variational-autoencoder loss. It estimates approximate hierarchies and encourages related subvolumes to lie closer together in the embedding space. The authors identify this objective as essential to capturing the relationships they seek. Experiments on synthetic data and a medical dataset support their hypothesis that representing implicit hierarchy benefits this segmentation setting. The contribution therefore combines a geometric choice with a training signal that encourages the intended structure.
neurips-2021-capturing-implicit-hierarch.tldr: A hyperbolic variational autoencoder uses self-supervised hierarchy learning to improve representations for unsupervised 3D biomedical segmentation.

paragraphs: Semi-supervised domain adaptation combines labeled source data with a target domain containing only a few labeled examples and additional unlabeled data. The paper argues that methods designed for a completely unlabeled target domain do not transfer well to this setting. There are two discrepancies to address: between source and target, and between the labeled and unlabeled portions of the target.

CLDA uses two complementary forms of contrastive learning. A class-wise component aims to reduce the discrepancy between source data and unlabeled target data. An instance-level component aligns each unlabeled target image with a strongly augmented version of itself, aiming to reduce the discrepancy within the target domain.

The authors empirically find that these components complement each other. Experiments on DomainNet, Office-Home, and Office31 report state-of-the-art results across all three benchmarks. The stated findings support addressing both discrepancies together: transferring class-related information across domains while making target representations consistent under strong image augmentation. The contribution is a simple combined training framework tailored to the availability of a small amount of target supervision.
neurips-2021-clda-contrastive-learning-f.tldr: CLDA combines class-wise and instance-level contrastive learning to address two gaps in semi-supervised domain adaptation.

paragraphs: Many time series contain only partial observations, recorded at irregular times. A model with continuous dynamics can represent what happens between observations and support inference at times absent from the recorded data. This paper addresses two challenges in such models: expressing sufficiently rich dynamics and constructing effective variational approximations for inference.

Continuous latent process flows connect a continuous hidden process to a continuous observable process. The architecture uses a time-dependent normalizing flow driven by a stochastic differential equation. This provides the model's mechanism for decoding latent dynamics into observations while retaining a continuous-time formulation.

The paper also develops a piecewise construction of the variational posterior process. Through trajectory reweighting, the authors derive a variational lower bound for likelihood-based training. Their ablation studies support the usefulness of these contributions across inference tasks on irregular time grids. Comparisons with state-of-the-art baselines show favorable performance on synthetic and real-world time series. Together, the architecture and inference procedure address both what continuous-time dynamics the model can represent and how it can learn from incomplete observations.
neurips-2021-continuous-latent-process-f.tldr: Continuous latent process flows combine stochastic dynamics, normalizing flows, and variational inference to model irregularly observed time series.

paragraphs: A conventional decision tree often divides the input space using one hyperplane at each internal node. Complex boundaries can consequently require many nodes. Convex polytope trees expand the kinds of splits available at a node while aiming to preserve an interpretable description of the decision boundary.

Each split combines a group of differently weighted probabilistic linear decision-makers through a logical disjunction. Geometrically, the construction corresponds to a convex polytope in the input space. A nonparametric Bayesian prior determines the size of this group and encourages simpler boundaries by shrinking the number of polytope facets. This lets the model adjust the complexity of individual splits.

The authors provide a greedy procedure for building the tree and scalable algorithms for jointly training its parameters once the structure is fixed. Experiments across real-world classification and regression tasks demonstrate efficiency relative to existing state-of-the-art decision trees. The approach therefore changes both the expressive capacity of a tree node and the way that capacity is controlled, rather than relying only on adding more nodes.
neurips-2021-convex-polytope-trees-f006f.tldr: Convex polytope trees learn more expressive, interpretable node boundaries while using Bayesian shrinkage to encourage simpler splits.

paragraphs: Dataset distillation seeks to compress a large training dataset into a much smaller collection that still supports effective learning. The challenge is to retain useful predictive information despite removing most of the original data volume. This paper approaches that challenge using infinitely wide convolutional neural networks within a distributed, kernel-based meta-learning framework.

The framework produces state-of-the-art distillation results in the reported settings. On CIFAR-10, a distilled dataset containing just ten data points—0.02% of the original dataset—supports test accuracy above 65%. The abstract contrasts this with a previous best of 40%, illustrating how much predictive value a very small distilled collection can retain in this setup.

The reported improvements extend across settings involving MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and SVHN. The authors also conduct preliminary analyses of how distilled examples differ from naturally occurring data. These findings make dataset compression relevant to training efficiency while emphasizing that the small dataset is optimized for its learning role. The analyses begin to examine what information such compressed collections contain.
neurips-2021-dataset-distillation-with-i.tldr: A distributed kernel-based framework distills image datasets into tiny collections with strong reported classification performance.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to extract and release sequences of text units, called n-grams, from a private corpus while preserving privacy at the user level. The objective is to release as many n-grams as possible under that privacy requirement. Such extraction is a building block for applications including sentence completion and automatic email responses.

The authors connect the task to differentially private set union, a related problem that n-gram extraction generalizes. Their algorithm combines advances in private set union with improved privacy accounting and new pruning heuristics for a tree-based extraction approach. The components address the shared challenge of finding useful sequences while managing the privacy implications of the overall procedure.

Experiments show that the resulting algorithm significantly outperforms the state of the art in the evaluated settings. The contribution is therefore a stronger extraction procedure assembled from complementary privacy and search techniques. Its relevance also extends beyond text: the abstract identifies sequence mining and trajectory analysis as applications where the same extraction problem arises. The stated goal remains useful release with user-level privacy, rather than unrestricted access to the underlying records.
neurips-2021-differentially-private-n-gr.tldr: A new private n-gram extractor combines set-union methods, privacy accounting, and tree pruning to improve empirical extraction performance.

paragraphs: Knowledge distillation trains a smaller object detector using information from a larger teacher, helping address deployment costs in computation and storage. This paper examines how to choose the teacher features worth transferring. Existing approaches that concentrate on features near bounding boxes can miss useful information outside them and copy features the teacher mistakenly treats as background.

The proposed Feature-Richness Score selects features according to their value for detection during distillation. The method retrieves useful features outside bounding boxes and removes detrimental ones inside them. Its central contribution is therefore a more selective transfer process, where location relative to a box is insufficient by itself to determine whether a feature should be imitated.

Experiments report strong performance for both anchor-based and anchor-free detectors. In one example on COCO2017, a RetinaNet student using ResNet-50 reaches 39.7% mean average precision, compared with 38.9% for its ResNet-101 teacher. That result shows that the smaller student can exceed its teacher in the reported setup, supporting the usefulness of choosing the transferred features carefully.
neurips-2021-distilling-object-detectors.tldr: Feature-Richness Score improves detector distillation by selecting useful teacher features both inside and outside bounding boxes.

paragraphs: Domain generalization asks a model trained on several source domains to perform well on unseen target domains. Simply pooling the source data can leave the model dependent on information specific to those sources. This paper pursues representations that preserve useful predictive information while remaining invariant across domains.

The proposed method expresses invariance through transformations between domains. It requires the representation network to remain unchanged under all such transformation functions. This gives the approach a concrete learning principle: domain changes represented by those transformations should not alter the learned representation. The authors present the method as theoretically grounded.

For a practical implementation, the paper introduces generative adversarial networks to learn the domain transformations. These learned transformations provide a way to put the invariance principle into a training procedure. Evaluations on several widely used domain-generalization datasets produce results competitive with state-of-the-art models on all of them. The findings support transformation-based invariance as an effective approach in the tested settings, with the adversarial implementation serving as one possible realization of the broader method.
neurips-2021-domain-invariant-representa.tldr: The method learns domain-invariant representations by enforcing consistency under transformations between source domains.

paragraphs: Active sequential hypothesis testing asks a learner to identify the true hypothesis by choosing actions and observing their outcomes. The candidate hypotheses and available actions are known, as is each action's outcome distribution under each hypothesis. The objective is to use as few actions as possible while keeping the probability of error below a specified target.

The paper develops efficient greedy algorithms for settings with very large numbers of hypotheses or actions. It supplies the first approximation guarantees for this problem under two forms of adaptivity. Both guarantees are independent of the number of available actions and depend only logarithmically on the number of hypotheses. This describes the scaling of the guarantees, rather than asserting that executing the algorithms has no dependence on the action set.

Numerical evaluations use synthetic data and real DNA mutation data. The proposed algorithms outperform previously suggested heuristic policies by large margins in these evaluations. The results combine a theoretical justification for greedy action selection with empirical evidence in a setting motivated by genomics-based cancer detection.
neurips-2021-greedy-approximation-algori.tldr: Greedy algorithms gain approximation guarantees and strong empirical results for identifying hypotheses through sequentially chosen actions.

paragraphs: An embodied agent needs to connect language with its observations and experiences. This paper introduces a task focused on descriptions that refer to space and time: a model must determine whether a description matches an agent's observation history. The descriptions include past and present tense, events extending over time, and references to objects in a scene.

The authors train a truth function for this matching task and compare several architectures. Their multimodal Transformers differ in how attention connects words and objects across spatial and temporal information. Evaluation examines two kinds of generalization: handling new sentences and generalizing to grammar primitives. This makes architectural choices part of the investigation into grounded language learning.

The experiments identify preservation of object identity during attention as instrumental to good overall generalization. By comparison, summarizing an object's trace in a single token has little effect on performance. These findings suggest that how the model maintains the connection to a particular object matters more in the tested task than that trace-summary choice. The paper discusses implications for language-guided autonomous embodied agents.
neurips-2021-grounding-spatio-temporal-l.tldr: A language-grounding task shows that preserving object identity in Transformer attention helps generalization across space and time.

paragraphs: Meta-learning can prepare a neural network to adapt from a small dataset by learning a useful starting set of weights. This paper extends that idea by allowing the learning algorithm to decide which weights should change during adaptation. The learned adaptation procedure therefore includes where learning takes place, alongside the initial parameter values.

The authors find that structured patterns of sparse updates emerge, and that these patterns differ between problems. This means the method does not impose one universally preferred subset of adaptable weights. In a range of few-shot and continual learning problems, the resulting selectivity improves generalization and reduces interference.

Sparse learning also emerges in a more expressive model that meta-learns learning rates. That observation supports the broader relevance of selective adaptation beyond the initial formulation. The findings contribute to the question of whether meta-learning can discover adaptable features, and suggest sparse gradient descent as a useful inductive bias. Their practical meaning is that restricting updates in a learned, problem-dependent way can improve adaptation in the evaluated settings.
neurips-2021-learning-where-to-learn-gra.tldr: Learning which weights to update produces problem-dependent sparsity that improves tested few-shot and continual learning outcomes.

paragraphs: Neural methods can support combinatorial optimization by extracting information from a problem's parameters to guide the search for good solutions. Many practical problems describe relationships between two groups of items using a matrix. This paper focuses on providing a neural architecture that can directly accept and process that form of relationship data.

The proposed Matrix Encoding Network, or MatNet, makes those matrix-valued parameters available to an end-to-end optimization model. The authors demonstrate it on the asymmetric traveling salesman problem and the flexible flow shop problem, presenting these applications as the earliest neural approaches to the two problems.

For a particular class of flexible flow shop problems tested in the paper, MatNet achieves substantially better empirical performance than the previously known methods considered, including non-neural ones. The scope of that result is the tested class, rather than every scheduling or combinatorial optimization problem. The broader contribution is an input-processing architecture that lets neural optimization methods work with problems naturally specified by relationships in a matrix.
neurips-2021-matrix-encoding-networks-fo.tldr: MatNet processes matrix-defined optimization problems and reports strong results on routing and a tested class of scheduling problems.

paragraphs: This paper develops a framework for understanding recurrent neural networks trained with noise added to their hidden states. It considers networks that can be interpreted as discrete approximations to stochastic differential equations driven by input data. This perspective connects the effects of noise during training with the dynamics of the recurrent model.

In the small-noise regime, the authors derive an approximate explicit regularizer corresponding to the otherwise implicit effect of noise injection. Under the stated assumptions of their analysis, this regularization encourages flatter minima, more stable dynamics, and larger classification margins. These are conditional conclusions about the analyzed framework, rather than guarantees for every possible noise scheme or recurrent network.

The paper also gives sufficient conditions for global stability and highlights stochastic stabilization: adding noise can improve stability during training. Empirical results support the theory by showing improved robustness to various input perturbations. Together, the analysis and experiments explain why hidden-state noise can serve as a useful training mechanism, with effects extending beyond simply making the training inputs to recurrent computations less predictable.
neurips-2021-noisy-recurrent-neural-netw.tldr: A stochastic-dynamics framework explains how hidden-state noise can regularize recurrent networks toward stability and robustness.

paragraphs: This paper studies predictive control when linear system dynamics and costs change over time. The costs are assumed to be well-conditioned, and the controller receives exact forecasts of costs, dynamics, and disturbances for the next k steps. The question is how the length of that prediction window affects stability and control performance.

For sufficiently large k, the authors prove input-to-state stability and a dynamic regret bound of O(λ^k T), with a positive constant λ below one. Because λ^k decreases exponentially as the window grows, the bound improves rapidly with additional exact lookahead. Its dependence on the overall duration T remains explicit.

A variation of predictive control also obtains a competitive bound of 1 + O(λ^k). The paper presents these as the first respective regret and competitive bounds for linear time-varying systems. Both results follow from a perturbation-based proof framework that tracks how small changes in system parameters affect the optimal trajectory. The conclusions apply to the stated forecasting setup, where the future information within the window is exact.
neurips-2021-perturbation-based-regret-a.tldr: With sufficiently long exact forecasts, predictive control gains stability and exponentially improving performance bounds for time-varying linear systems.

paragraphs: Contrastive learning often treats two augmented versions of one image as a positive pair. Those versions can remain strongly dependent even after their class is specified, which conflicts with an independence assumption used in earlier theoretical analyses. This paper develops guarantees without requiring that conditional independence.

The authors introduce an augmentation graph whose edges connect augmentations of the same underlying example. Ground-truth classes form connected subgraphs in this view. They propose an objective that performs a spectral decomposition of the population augmentation graph while also having a compact contrastive formulation for neural representations. The graph connects the structure of augmentation relationships to the representation-learning objective.

Minimizing this objective yields provable accuracy guarantees when the learned features are evaluated with a linear probe. Standard generalization bounds extend those guarantees to minimizing the training contrastive loss. The result supplies a theoretical account that can apply to more realistic positive-pair constructions. Its contribution concerns the proposed spectral objective and associated analysis, rather than a guarantee that every contrastive objective produces accurate representations.
neurips-2021-provable-guarantees-for-sel.tldr: An augmentation-graph analysis gives linear-probe accuracy guarantees for spectral contrastive learning without conditional independence of positive pairs.

paragraphs: Optimal transport seeks a coupling that connects a source distribution to a target distribution optimally. In some cases this connection is a one-to-one map, but learning such maps can be computationally difficult for large, high-dimensional datasets. This paper instead studies the Sinkhorn problem, a regularized version whose solution is a coupling between distributions.

The authors represent that regularized coupling using a score-based generative model. Given a source example, their procedure runs Langevin dynamics to sample a target example according to the learned regularized transport coupling. The goal is therefore to generate target samples conditioned on source data, rather than explicitly recover a one-to-one transport map.

A neural-network parameterization of the Sinkhorn problem is central to the framework. The paper proves convergence of gradient descent with respect to the network parameters in that formulation and demonstrates empirical success on several large-scale transport tasks. The theoretical and experimental contributions address complementary parts of the approach: learning the parameterized problem and using its coupling for conditional sampling at scale.
neurips-2021-score-based-generative-neur.tldr: A score-based generative framework learns regularized transport couplings and samples target data conditioned on source examples.

paragraphs: Recognizing a scene can require evidence spread across an image. This paper examines scene-classification networks through their focus area: the regions they activate when learning scene characteristics. The authors find that a larger focus area is preferred for this task and use that observation to design a training scheme.

Because training usually lacks labels specifying which additional regions should become active, the method erases areas the network already activates. It then encourages consistency between the predictions for the erased image and the original image. A tailored loss uses category-relevance information to maintain this consistency, allowing the network to activate more of the remaining scene during training.

Experiments on Places365 show significant improvements across several convolutional networks. The method performs worse on the object-centered ImageNet dataset, which the authors interpret as evidence that it captures properties specific to scenes. The findings support broadening attention when category information is distributed across the image, while the reported ImageNet result keeps that empirical benefit tied to the scene-classification setting.
neurips-2021-see-more-for-scene-pairwise.tldr: Erasing activated regions and enforcing prediction consistency encourages broader scene focus and improves reported Places365 performance.

paragraphs: Technical CAD designs often begin as two-dimensional sketches containing geometric primitives and constraints. Points, lines, and arcs supply the geometry, while relationships such as coincidence, parallelism, and orthogonality connect them. Generating these sketches is difficult because different primitive and constraint types require records with different lengths and parameter types.

SketchGen addresses this heterogeneity with a transformer-based generative model and a carefully designed sequential language. The language distinguishes the kinds of primitives and constraints and their parameters while encouraging shared information across related parameters. This gives the model a way to generate the different records within a common representation.

A key feature is that the output includes constraints linking the generated primitives. A constraint solver can subsequently regularize the sketch using those relationships. The authors evaluate both prediction of constraints for supplied primitives and generation of complete sketches from scratch, reporting substantial improvements over the state of the art. The contribution therefore concerns structured, constrained CAD content, including relationships that remain useful after the generative model has produced its output.
neurips-2021-sketchgen-generating-constr.tldr: SketchGen uses a transformer and a structured sequence language to generate CAD primitives together with geometric constraints.

paragraphs: Approximate nearest-neighbor search becomes expensive when a very large index must fit in memory. SPANN divides the index between memory and an inexpensive solid-state drive. It keeps the centroids representing posting lists in memory and stores the much larger lists themselves on disk, aiming for fast search with a smaller memory footprint.

The system addresses disk access during both index construction and querying. Hierarchical balanced clustering controls posting-list lengths, and the lists are augmented with points from the corresponding cluster closures. At query time, a query-aware pruning scheme avoids accessing unnecessary lists. These choices aim to retrieve useful candidates while reducing disk accesses.

Across three billion-scale datasets, SPANN is reported to be twice as fast as DiskANN at 90% recall with the same memory cost. The abstract also reports roughly one-millisecond search at 90% recall@1 and recall@10 using about 10% of the original memory cost. These empirical results demonstrate the value of coordinating index organization and query pruning in a memory-disk search system.
neurips-2021-spann-highly-efficient-bill.tldr: SPANN combines memory-resident centroids, disk-based posting lists, and query-aware pruning for fast billion-scale approximate search.

paragraphs: Uniform stability describes how sensitive a learning algorithm is to changes in its training data. Existing high-probability generalization bounds for stable algorithms include a sampling-error term of order 1/√n. Although generally unavoidable for those bounds, that term can give overly slow excess-risk guarantees in standard stochastic convex optimization problems.

The paper shows that the Bernstein condition allows this obstacle to be avoided when bounding excess risk. Under that condition, uniform stability can yield high-probability rates as fast as O(1/n). The distinction matters: the result concerns excess risk under an additional condition, rather than removing the sampling term from every generalization problem.

As an application, the authors establish an O(log n/n) high-probability excess-risk bound for any empirical risk minimization method with strongly convex, Lipschitz losses. They also discuss obtaining that rate for projected gradient descent under the same loss properties without the usual smoothness assumption. These results strengthen what stability analysis can establish about optimization and learning when the stated structural conditions hold.
neurips-2021-stability-and-deviation-opt.tldr: Under the Bernstein condition, stability analysis can yield faster high-probability excess-risk bounds, reaching O(1/n) in suitable settings.

paragraphs: This paper introduces a multidimensional differential privacy mechanism using Skellam noise, formed by subtracting two independent Poisson random variables. Its discrete values make it relevant to settings where communication limits the precision of transmitted information. The authors focus on federated learning with secure aggregation, while also considering centralized and distributed privacy applications.

To characterize privacy, they numerically examine the privacy-loss distribution and derive a sharp bound on the Rényi divergence between shifted Skellam distributions. Their theoretical findings and experiments show the same privacy-accuracy tradeoffs as the continuous Gaussian mechanism, including at low precision in the investigated settings.

The mechanism also has practical structural advantages. Sums of Skellam variables remain within the Skellam family, and generating the noise requires Poisson sampling, an efficient routine available in machine-learning and data-analysis software. Those properties support distributed noise generation and aggregation. Combined with its discrete form and reported privacy-accuracy behavior, they make Skellam noise a practical alternative to the discrete Gaussian mechanism discussed in the paper.
neurips-2021-the-skellam-mechanism-for-d.tldr: Skellam noise offers discrete, efficiently sampled privacy protection with competitive privacy-accuracy tradeoffs for federated learning.

paragraphs: A ranking model can score well on overall area under the ROC curve while performing poorly where false positives must remain rare. This paper instead targets the true-positive rate at a specified false-positive rate, called TPR@FPR, for multipartite ranking. That metric focuses learning on the operating region relevant to these applications.

Direct optimization has two obstacles. The objective is not differentiable, and its loss cannot be separated into independent terms for individual examples. The proposed Cross-Batch Approximation for Multipartite Ranking framework addresses the first obstacle with a differentiable surrogate. Under a random-walk hypothesis, it assigns different weights to examples according to their short-term effects on the false-positive rate.

To address the second obstacle, the method estimates rankings using an embedding cache and delayed updates, replacing full-batch loss evaluation. This makes the ranking objective workable within the proposed deep-learning framework. Experiments on four real-world benchmarks demonstrate its effectiveness. The contribution joins an operating-point-specific objective with approximations that address both gradient-based training and the dependence of rankings on examples beyond an individual mini-batch.
neurips-2021-when-false-positive-is-into.tldr: CBA-MR makes low-false-positive-rate ranking optimization practical through a differentiable surrogate and cached cross-batch ranking estimates.

paragraphs: Disentanglement aims to recover the independent factors underlying high-dimensional observations without labeled examples of those factors. Such recovery is impossible in general without additional assumptions. This paper establishes a sufficient combination: local isometry, which preserves local geometry, together with non-Gaussian latent factors. These conditions make provable recovery possible in the studied setting.

The authors use deep generative models to construct manifolds of realistic images with known latent representations. That known structure lets them test whether learning methods recover the underlying factors. Across many of these manifolds, a spectral method explicitly optimizing local isometry and non-Gaussianity consistently recovers the factors, while the baseline deep autoencoders do not.

The paper then proposes encouraging deep autoencoders to satisfy local isometry and shows that this helps them discover disentangled representations. The findings identify structural assumptions that can enable recovery without domain-specific assumptions. They do not establish that those conditions are necessary or that arbitrary unlabeled data are disentangleable; the positive conclusion is that recovery is provably possible in some realistic settings.
neurips-2021-when-is-unsupervised-disent.tldr: Local isometry and non-Gaussian factors are sufficient for provable unsupervised disentanglement in the studied setting.
